newsitem.title: USA: U.S. in new Israel-Palestinian mediation.
newsitem.headline: U.S. in new Israel-Palestinian mediation.

text.p: The United States said on Monday it was sharing ideas and trying to mediate anew on peace between Israelis and Palestinians but refused to comment on reports of a proposed "package deal" of measures to break the deadlock.

"The United States is trying to do what it always tries to do. We're trying to be an effective mediator between the Palestinians and the Israelis," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said of a flurry of new Mideast activity.
"And obviously, we'll share our own ideas and listen to theirs about how the peace process can move forward," he added.

Israeli leader Benjamin Netanyahu said on Monday he was sending a senior adviser, Cabinet Secretary Danny Naveh, to Washington with proposals for ending a four-month-old peacemaking crisis with Palestinians. He did not elaborate.

This follows a trip to Washington last week by Palestinian negotiator Saeb Erekat for talks with U.S. Mideast Coordinator Dennis Ross and Undersecretary of State Thomas Pickering, who years ago was ambassador to Israel and also to Jordan.

"The main objective of these talks is quite simple. It is to promote the willingness of both sides to move forward with the type of face-to-face meetings, discussions that will allow the peace negotiations to succeed and to allow the Oslo accords to succeed," Burns told reporters.

Israeli-PLO talks, launched with a U.S.-backed interim accord in 1993, have been stuck since Netanyahu started building a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem in March, triggering Palestinian protests.
On Saturday, Erekat said Washington was preparing a "package deal" of measures to end the deadlock. But Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat said on Sunday there were as yet no new U.S. initiatives.

Burns refused to say if a "package deal" of measures was on the table or even being considered "because that would violate our cardinal rule here, and that is, we don't speak in public about specifics of what we're talking about."
"The United States is acting as we always do ... We're urging political dialogue and reconciliation," he said.
He insisted Arafat and Netanyahu "want to preserve the Oslo accords and want to move forward" but said "the difficulty is in arranging a specific way to do that."
The aim is face-to-face talks between the two leaders, he added.
Netanyahu has demanded Palestinians do more to crack down on Moslem guerrillas opposed to Israeli-PLO peace accords.
There has also been trouble over Palestinian justice minister Freih Abu Meddein who advocated death for Palestinians suspected of selling land to Israelis.
Palestinian officials said Monday Abu Meddein had resigned and Burns said "I'm not sure there are many tears being shed" over the minister's departure.
Arafat is due to appoint a replacement and "we hope to work very closely and amicably with that person," Burns said.

The United States has spoken out strongly against what it called "political assassination against people who sell land to Israelis." While Arafat some time ago also strongly opposed such violence, Burns said with Abu Meddein's departure "perhaps that prospect is more sure now."
